idiom_name: struct with an embedded _Atomic count + buf_ref/buf_unref pair (kref/GObject shape)
implementation_notes: C has no destructors, copy constructors or smart pointers, so the whole structure is written by hand: the body struct carries the count (an _Atomic counter from <stdatomic.h>, or struct kref in kernel code), the creation function initialises it to 1, and a ref/unref pair performs the increment and the decrement-then-release. What replaces the C++ handle's copy/destroy hooks: the calling convention - every owner must call buf_ref when it stores a pointer and buf_unref on every exit path, so the discipline a compiler enforces in C++ becomes a documented protocol here. Where the ecosystem already provides the mechanism (GLib's g_object_ref/g_object_unref for GObject-derived types, the kernel's kref for kernel objects), reuse it instead of inventing a second convention.
pitfalls: Every early return and error path must buf_unref; C has no scope-exit hook, so a missed release leaks and a double release is a use-after-free.

A plain unsigned count (no _Atomic, no lock) shared across threads is a data race; even with atomics the last decrement needs acquire/release ordering so the body's writes are visible before it is freed.
A second count for one body - for example a struct copied by value while its pointer is also shared - double-frees; ref/unref must operate only on the one counted struct.
